lessons.title: Network sizes: PAN to WAN
lessons.core: A network is a collection of connected devices. PAN covers a person and nearby devices; LAN covers a home or office; CAN connects nearby campus buildings; MAN serves a metro area; WAN links distant sites. The Internet is a global interconnection of networks, not simply one giant LAN.
lessons.example: A phone paired with earbuds is a PAN. Multiple floors in one office commonly share a LAN. A corporate private link from Atlanta to London is part of a WAN.
lessons.trap: Do not decide from device count alone. Geographic span, ownership and purpose are better clues.
lessons.tip: Memory ladder: Personal, Local, Campus, Metro, Wide. Move outward as distance grows.
lessons.scenario: An organization connects its offices in two different states with a carrier circuit. Which network scope best fits?
options: PAN
LAN
MAN
WAN
lessons.hint: Focus on how far the connected sites extend.

lessons.title: Star, bus, ring and mesh
lessons.core: Topology describes how nodes are arranged. A star connects devices to a central switch. A bus shares a backbone cable. A ring links devices around a loop. A full mesh gives every node a direct path to every other node; it maximizes path choice but requires many links.
lessons.example: If one cable to a workstation fails in a star, that workstation loses connectivity while its peers may continue. If the shared bus backbone breaks, multiple devices can be affected.
lessons.trap: Physical layout and logical traffic flow need not be identical. A switch-based Ethernet LAN is commonly a physical star.
lessons.tip: Memory: star has a center, ring has a circle, bus has one shared road, mesh has many roads.
lessons.scenario: Which topology uses individual links from workstations to one central switch?

Ring
Star
Full mesh

lessons.title: OSI layers and encapsulation
lessons.core: The OSI model separates network work into seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. Frames are a Data Link concept, packets are a Network concept, and TCP or UDP segments and datagrams are Transport concepts. Encapsulation adds headers as data travels down the stack.
lessons.example: A router forwards IP packets at Layer 3; a switch commonly forwards Ethernet frames at Layer 2. An app request travels down through several layers before bits cross the medium.
lessons.trap: Layers describe responsibilities, not necessarily seven separate physical boxes.
lessons.tip: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application: work upward from the cable to the user.
lessons.scenario: A device chooses the next hop using a destination IP address. Which OSI layer makes this decision?
options: Data Link
Network
Transport
Session
lessons.hint: Decide whether the address identifies a local interface or a routed network.

lessons.title: Switches, routers and access points
lessons.core: A typical Ethernet switch uses MAC addresses to forward frames within a LAN. A router uses IP networks to move packets between subnets. A wireless access point bridges Wi-Fi clients into a wired or wireless LAN. A hub repeats electrical traffic to every port instead of selectively forwarding it.
lessons.example: A user can reach local printers but not a different subnet: investigate the default gateway or routing rather than immediately replacing the access point.
lessons.trap: A consumer Wi-Fi router may combine a switch, router, firewall and access point in one enclosure.
lessons.tip: Memory: Switch stays local, Router reaches other networks, AP brings radio clients onto the LAN.

lessons.title: Bandwidth, throughput, latency, jitter and loss
lessons.core: Bandwidth is the capacity of a link; throughput is the useful rate achieved. Latency is how long a packet takes to travel; jitter is variation in that delay; packet loss is missing traffic. High throughput does not guarantee a good real-time phone call because voice is highly sensitive to delay variation and loss.
lessons.example: A speed test reads 900 Mbps, yet callers sound robotic. The bottleneck may be jitter or packet loss, not bandwidth.
lessons.trap: Do not confuse bandwidth with speed of individual packets or jitter with ordinary total delay.
lessons.tip: Memory: Bandwidth is pipe size, throughput is actual flow, latency is travel time, jitter is inconsistent timing.
lessons.scenario: A VoIP call has uneven audio arrival times despite adequate bandwidth. Which metric is most directly implicated?
options: Jitter
Maximum cable length
MTU
Address scope
lessons.hint: Focus on variation rather than average capacity.

lessons.title: Analog and digital transmission
lessons.core: Analog signals vary continuously, while digital systems represent information using discrete symbols. Either kind of information can be transported using analog waveforms or encoded digital symbols, depending on the system. Converting an analog voice waveform to a digital stream normally requires sampling and quantization.
lessons.example: A microphone captures a continuously varying sound pressure wave. A digital telephone converts that waveform into samples for processing and transport.

lessons.title: Attenuation, noise, distortion and SNR
lessons.core: Attenuation is the reduction of signal strength as it travels. Noise is unwanted energy mixed into a signal; distortion changes the signal shape. Signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, compares useful signal power with noise power. More useful signal relative to noise generally makes decoding easier, though thresholds depend on modulation and coding.
lessons.example: A long cable run introduces attenuation; an electric motor may inject interference; a damaged connector can cause reflections and distortion.
lessons.trap: An amplifier can raise both the desired signal and the noise already present. It cannot magically restore missing information.
lessons.tip: Memory: attenuation shrinks, noise intrudes, distortion reshapes, SNR compares.

options: SNR

RTT
lessons.hint: The name describes a ratio between two kinds of energy.

lessons.title: ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM
lessons.core: Modulation changes a carrier to represent information. ASK changes amplitude, FSK changes frequency, and PSK changes phase. QAM combines amplitude and phase choices to carry more bits per symbol in many modern systems. Higher-order constellations can raise data rate but normally demand cleaner channels.
lessons.example: Wi-Fi commonly uses forms of QAM on OFDM subcarriers. When a radio link gets noisy, it may choose a lower-order constellation for reliability.
lessons.trap: Do not equate higher-order modulation with automatically better real-world throughput under poor signal conditions.
lessons.tip: Memory: A is amplitude, F is frequency, P is phase; QAM uses amplitude plus phase.

lessons.title: FDM, TDM and WDM
lessons.core: Multiplexing carries several logical channels over one physical resource. Frequency-division multiplexing, FDM, assigns distinct frequency bands. Time-division multiplexing, TDM, gives channels different time slots. Wavelength-division multiplexing, WDM, puts different wavelengths, or colors, of light on a fiber. All three separate users but in different dimensions.

lessons.tip: Memory: F for frequency, T for turns in time, W for wavelengths of light.

lessons.title: Twisted pair categories
lessons.core: Balanced twisted-pair Ethernet cabling uses wire pairs twisted to reduce interference. Common channel lengths are up to 100 meters for many twisted-pair Ethernet variants. Cat5e commonly supports 1 Gbps over 100 meters. Cat6a is widely used for 10GBASE-T over 100 meters; Cat6 can carry 10 Gbps only over shorter runs depending on the environment.
lessons.example: An office planning 10-gigabit links from the rack to desks at 90 meters should consider Cat6a rather than assuming Cat6 always reaches that distance.
lessons.trap: Category frequency ratings are not themselves connection speeds, and performance depends on installation quality.
lessons.tip: Memory: 6A adds margin for ten gig across the full hundred meters.

lessons.title: Single-mode versus multimode fiber
lessons.core: Fiber transmits light pulses rather than electrical current. Single-mode fiber has a small core supporting a primary light mode and is suited to long distances, often with laser transmitters. Multimode fiber has a larger core and is common for shorter in-building data center or campus links. Different optics and fiber types have different reach specifications.
lessons.example: A multi-kilometer building-to-building carrier link is generally a strong candidate for single-mode fiber.
lessons.trap: Fiber is resistant to electromagnetic interference but still faces attenuation, bending loss and dirty end faces.
lessons.tip: Memory: Single-mode for distance, multimode for many short-run enterprise links.

lessons.core: Optical transceivers convert between electrical data and optical signals. SFP and related pluggable module families provide interfaces with specific speeds, wavelengths and reaches. lessons.title: WDM and optical link budgets
lessons.core: In wavelength-division multiplexing, separate optical channels use different wavelengths on the same fiber. Dense WDM packs channels closely to increase capacity. An optical link budget subtracts losses from transmitter output and compares the remaining received power with receiver sensitivity. Splices, connectors, splitters and fiber length all contribute loss.

lessons.title: Ethernet and IEEE 802.3

lessons.title: MAC addresses, frames and ARP
lessons.core: A MAC address identifies a network interface at the Data Link layer. Switches learn source MAC locations and use a table to forward unicast frames. ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a local-link MAC address so a host can send an Ethernet frame to the right next hop.
lessons.example: A workstation wants to reach its default gateway on the same Ethernet LAN. It may send an ARP request to learn the gateway interface MAC address.
lessons.trap: ARP does not resolve hostnames; DNS does that. ARP also does not route between subnets.
lessons.tip: Memory: DNS asks for a name-to-IP; ARP asks for an IPv4-to-MAC on the local link.

lessons.title: CSMA/CD versus CSMA/CA
lessons.core: Classic shared half-duplex Ethernet used carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection, CSMA/CD. Wireless LANs use collision avoidance, CSMA/CA, because a station generally cannot reliably detect a collision while transmitting its own radio signal. Modern full-duplex switched Ethernet does not rely on CSMA/CD for normal operation.
lessons.example: On busy Wi-Fi, devices attempt to coordinate access to a shared radio channel rather than expecting to hear every collision directly.
lessons.trap: Collision detection and collision avoidance are different. Their names describe the underlying medium access strategy.
lessons.tip: Memory: Ethernet hubs Detected, wireless Avoids.

lessons.title: SONET/SDH and redundancy
lessons.core: SONET and SDH are synchronous optical transport frameworks designed for high-capacity, organized carrier traffic. They can employ ring arrangements with alternate paths and protection switching. They are historically important in metropolitan and wide-area carrier networks, even as Ethernet and packet-based transport have expanded.
lessons.example: When a protected optical ring loses one fiber span, protection mechanisms may restore the circuit by moving traffic over the alternate ring direction.
lessons.trap: Being optical does not automatically make a connection SONET. The transport framing and architecture are the clues.
lessons.tip: Memory: SONET is synchronous optical carrier transport; ring protection helps survive cuts.
lessons.scenario: A legacy carrier optical ring automatically reroutes traffic after a fiber cut. Which architecture is associated with this?
options: DOCSIS
SONET/SDH protection ring
Bluetooth mesh
ADSL

lessons.title: Circuit switching versus packet switching
lessons.core: Circuit switching reserves or establishes a dedicated path or resource for a call during its lifetime, as in classic telephone systems. Packet switching divides data into packets that share network resources with other traffic. Packet switching is efficient for bursty data but can experience congestion, delay variation and loss.
lessons.example: A traditional PSTN call established a circuit-like connection, while a modern IP video call shares packet network bandwidth with other applications.
lessons.trap: Voice can travel on packet networks. A real-time application is not automatically circuit-switched.

lessons.title: Antenna gain, directionality and polarization
lessons.core: Antenna gain describes how an antenna concentrates radiation in a given direction relative to a reference, usually dBi. An omnidirectional antenna spreads energy around its horizontal plane; a directional antenna focuses energy into a smaller angular area. Polarization describes the orientation of the electromagnetic field and should match at each end for best results.

lessons.trap: An antenna does not create energy. Higher gain usually trades coverage angle for focus.
lessons.tip: Memory: gain reshapes energy, direction points it, polarization aligns it.

lessons.title: WPA2, WPA3 and authentication
lessons.core: Wi-Fi security uses authentication and encryption to protect wireless traffic. WPA2-Personal commonly uses a pre-shared passphrase with AES-CCMP. WPA3-Personal uses SAE for more robust password-based authentication. Enterprise deployments may use 802.1X with an authentication server. Protected Management Frames are important in modern secure WLAN configurations.
lessons.example: A company with individual employee credentials and centralized policy normally favors an enterprise authentication design rather than one shared office password.
lessons.trap: The SSID name alone tells you nothing about encryption strength. A hidden SSID is not a substitute for proper security.
lessons.tip: Memory: WPA3-Personal brings SAE; Enterprise points to per-user authentication.

lessons.title: Cells, sectors and frequency reuse
lessons.core: Cellular systems divide coverage into cells served by base stations. Sectors divide a site into directional service areas. Frequency reuse lets separated coverage areas use the same spectrum efficiently while managing interference. Cell size and capacity depend on frequency, terrain, buildings, demand and infrastructure.

lessons.title: From 2G and 3G to 4G LTE
lessons.core: Cellular generations mark major shifts. 2G introduced digital cellular voice technologies and SMS at scale. 3G increased mobile data capability. 4G LTE uses an all-IP packet data architecture and higher spectral efficiency, with voice often provided using VoLTE. lessons.title: GEO, MEO and LEO orbits
lessons.core: Geostationary satellites, GEO, orbit far above Earth at roughly 35,786 kilometers and appear fixed relative to the ground, allowing stationary dishes but with considerable propagation delay. Medium Earth orbit, MEO, falls between GEO and low Earth orbit, LEO. LEO satellites fly much lower, often reducing delay but requiring moving constellation coverage.
lessons.example: A satellite Internet system using many rapidly moving low-orbit satellites can often achieve much lower propagation latency than a traditional GEO system.
lessons.trap: Orbit choice affects latency and coverage but network architecture and congestion also influence real service quality.
lessons.tip: Memory: GEO high and fixed, LEO low and moving, MEO in the middle.

lessons.title: Microwave backhaul and line of sight
lessons.core: Terrestrial point-to-point microwave links use directional antennas to connect fixed sites. Many such links need a clear line of sight and adequate Fresnel-zone clearance. Trees, buildings and Earth curvature can obstruct paths, while changing weather affects some bands. The link must have sufficient fade margin to remain reliable.
lessons.example: A tower-to-tower wireless backhaul works in winter but degrades when summer tree growth blocks part of the path.
lessons.trap: An unobstructed visual line can still have poor RF performance if the Fresnel zone is obstructed.
lessons.tip: Memory: check the clear path, Fresnel zone, alignment and fade margin.
lessons.scenario: Which condition is most important for a point-to-point microwave path over several kilometers?
options: Clear line of sight and Fresnel-zone clearance
A shared VLAN name
A DOCSIS modem
A T1 framing bit

lessons.title: Bluetooth, Zigbee and LPWAN
lessons.core: Bluetooth is common for short-range personal connections such as headsets and peripherals. Zigbee, based on IEEE 802.15.4, targets low-power mesh-capable device networks in many IoT applications. LPWAN technologies such as LoRaWAN trade data rate for low power consumption and long coverage, useful for sensors that send occasional small messages.
lessons.example: A battery-powered environmental sensor sending a few bytes several times a day across a large property may benefit from an LPWAN approach.
lessons.trap: Do not choose a high-bandwidth Wi-Fi solution automatically for devices whose main constraint is battery life.
lessons.tip: Memory: Bluetooth is personal, Zigbee is low-power mesh, LPWAN is long-range sparse telemetry.
lessons.scenario: Which wireless approach best suits tiny sensor messages over long distances with minimal power?
options: LoRaWAN-style LPWAN
Wi-Fi 7 at 320 MHz
HDMI cable
10GBASE-T copper
lessons.hint: Prioritize distance, battery life and the very small payload.

lessons.title: TCP versus UDP in real-time voice
lessons.core: TCP is connection-oriented and provides ordered, reliable byte-stream delivery with retransmissions. UDP is connectionless and does not itself guarantee delivery or ordering. Real-time voice media commonly uses RTP over UDP because late retransmitted audio can be less useful than the next timely packet. Application-layer design determines how losses are handled.
lessons.example: A live call can tolerate a tiny missing sound better than waiting a second for old voice packets to be resent in strict order.
lessons.trap: UDP does not mean unencrypted or always faster under every condition; the advantage is avoiding transport-layer retransmission delay.
lessons.tip: Memory: TCP retries, UDP prioritizes timeliness for many media flows.

lessons.title: SIP signaling versus RTP media

lessons.title: Jitter buffers, codecs and QoS
lessons.core: A voice codec converts audio into a compressed or uncompressed stream using a particular format. A jitter buffer temporarily holds arriving packets to smooth variation in arrival time, trading some delay for continuity. Quality of Service can prioritize sensitive traffic and manage contention. No buffer can fully repair long gaps or massive packet loss.
lessons.example: A call sounds choppy at peak network hours despite plenty of nominal download capacity. Check loss and jitter, voice priority and the network bottleneck.
lessons.trap: Increasing jitter buffering indefinitely adds latency, which can make two-way conversations awkward.
lessons.tip: Memory: codec encodes, jitter buffer evens timing, QoS prioritizes.

lessons.title: PBX, ACD, SIP trunk and call flow

An automatic call distributor, ACD, routes inbound calls to suitable queues or agents. SIP trunking connects a PBX or other voice platform with telephony service through IP-based signaling. lessons.core: Network segmentation separates traffic into logical groups and applies policy at boundaries. lessons.title: Redundancy, availability and failover
lessons.core: Redundancy uses extra links, devices or services so a single failure does not necessarily cause an outage. Failover moves service to an alternate resource. lessons.title: Error detection: parity, checksum and CRC
lessons.core: Error detection attaches or calculates redundant information so a receiver can identify damaged data. Parity is a simple check of bit patterns. A checksum summarizes data according to a defined calculation. A cyclic redundancy check, CRC, is effective at detecting many common bit-error patterns and is used in Ethernet frames.

lessons.title: Systematic troubleshooting by layer
lessons.core: A disciplined workflow gathers symptoms, determines scope, tests a plausible cause, implements a fix and verifies the result. Starting low in the stack helps: power and link status, physical medium, local addresses and VLANs, routing, transport, then application services. Keep evidence of what changed.
lessons.example: An entire office loses connectivity immediately after fiber maintenance. Start with optics, light levels and port status rather than resetting every application.
lessons.trap: A strong theory is not proof. Use a discriminating test and avoid changing several variables at once.
lessons.tip: Memory: scope, physical, local link, IP path, transport, application, verify.
lessons.scenario: After a technician replaces a patch cable, every endpoint on a switch goes offline. What is the best first action?
options: Check physical link and switch status
Change all DNS servers
Reinstall client applications
Replace the WAN contract
lessons.hint: Choose the lowest-cost test closest to the recent change.

lessons.title: Copper and optical cable testing
lessons.core: Cable problems include opens, shorts, incorrect pinouts, excessive length, pair faults, bad termination, bending and optical insertion loss. A copper cable tester can reveal wiring faults; a certification tester measures category compliance. Optical power meters and OTDR tools help assess fiber loss and fault location.
lessons.example: A copper port negotiates down to 100 Mbps instead of 1 Gbps: a damaged or missing pair can be a reason because gigabit twisted-pair Ethernet needs all four pairs.
lessons.trap: A successful continuity beep does not guarantee a high-speed cable meets transmission performance requirements.
lessons.tip: Memory: test copper pinout and category; test fiber light loss and reflections.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Wi-Fi without guessing
lessons.core: Wireless troubleshooting should separate signal strength, signal quality, channel contention, client capability, roaming and upstream network performance. Measure RSSI and SNR where relevant, review channel plans, compare wired and wireless tests, and check whether the problem affects one device or many.
lessons.example: A laptop reports full signal bars but slow service during busy hours. Measuring channel utilization and interference is more informative than automatically replacing the ISP.
lessons.trap: Signal bars are a rough indicator and can hide heavy contention or a poor uplink.
lessons.tip: Memory: bars are not bandwidth; measure strength, quality, airtime and upstream.

options: Channel interference and contention

Optical splice tray
lessons.hint: Good strength does not rule out crowded radio airtime.
